primary_sources: David Walker, Appeal to the Coloured Citizens of the World, 1829
William Lloyd Garrison, "To the Public," The Liberator, 1831
Sarah Grimké, Letters on the Equality of the Sexes, 1838

source: original; documents are public-domain primary sources or paraphrases of them (see each document's sourcing note)
prompt: Evaluate the extent to which the abolition movement transformed the debate over slavery in the United States in the period 1817–1860.

documents.title: A society for colonization
documents.source: Paraphrase of Barron's Premium 2027, Chapter 6, Topic 4.11, B. Debating the Future of Slavery in America: the American Colonization Society.
documents.sourcing: A new society proposes sending free Black Americans to Africa.
documents.text: In 1817, the American Colonization Society was founded to transport free African Americans to Africa. Its founders disagreed about why: some hoped to free Black people from American racism, while others wanted to rid the country of free Black people altogether.

documents.title: Walker's Appeal
documents.source: Paraphrase of David Walker, Appeal to the Coloured Citizens of the World (Boston, 1829). Public domain.
documents.sourcing: A free Black Bostonian calls on Black Americans to resist slavery.
documents.text: Walker, a free Black man in Boston, urged enslaved people to resist their enslavement and free Black people to fight for abolition. His pamphlet reached the South and alarmed slaveholders, who saw it as a call to rebellion.

documents.title: Garrison's vow
documents.source: William Lloyd Garrison, "To the Public," The Liberator, January 1, 1831. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: An abolitionist editor promises uncompromising language.
documents.text: "I will be as harsh as truth, and as uncompromising as justice. On this subject, I do not wish to think, or speak, or write, with moderation."

documents.title: The Lovejoy murder
documents.source: Paraphrase of Barron's Premium 2027, Chapter 6, Topic 4.11, C. Growing Tensions over Slavery: the Lovejoy incident.
documents.sourcing: A mob kills an abolitionist editor in Illinois.
documents.text: In 1837, a proslavery mob in Alton, Illinois, killed the abolitionist newspaper publisher Elijah Lovejoy. Mobs had destroyed his printing press three times before they killed him.

documents.title: Grimké on equality
documents.source: Sarah Grimké, Letters on the Equality of the Sexes, 1838. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: An abolitionist argues that women's equality follows from antislavery.
documents.text: "But I ask no favors for my sex. I surrender not our claim to equality. All I ask of our brethren is, that they will take their feet from off our necks, and permit us to stand upright on that ground which God designed us to occupy."

documents.title: The Fugitive Slave Act
documents.source: Fugitive Slave Act of 1850, Section 5, approved September 18, 1850. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: Congress orders every citizen to help return escaped slaves.
documents.text: In 1850, Congress passed the Fugitive Slave Act, which required the return of people who had escaped slavery. Its fifth section commanded that "all good citizens are hereby commanded to aid and assist in the prompt and efficient execution of this law." Northerners who had ignored the debate now faced it in their own towns.

documents.title: Dred Scott
documents.source: Dred Scott v. Sandford, 60 U.S. 393 (1857), opinion of Chief Justice Roger Taney. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: The Supreme Court rules that Black people are not citizens.
documents.text: In 1857, Chief Justice Roger Taney, writing for the Supreme Court in Dred Scott v. Sandford, ruled that Black people were not citizens and could not sue in federal court. Looking back to the founding era, he wrote that Black people had been regarded as beings of an inferior order, so far inferior "that they had no rights which the white man was bound to respect."

rubric.criterion: Thesis: earns the point for a historically defensible claim that answers the prompt, stating the extent to which the abolition movement transformed the debate over slavery, with a clear line of reasoning.
rubric.notEarned: Restating the prompt with no claim about the extent of change does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Contextualization: earns the point for describing a broader historical context relevant to the prompt, such as the Second Great Awakening, the market revolution, or the expansion of white male democracy.
rubric.notEarned: A sentence of background with no link to the argument does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Evidence from documents (first point): earns the point for describing the content of at least three documents relevant to the argument.
rubric.notEarned: Quoting documents without describing what they show does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Evidence from documents (second point): earns the point for using the content of at least six documents to support the argument.
rubric.notEarned: Using fewer than six documents, or using six without tying them to the argument, does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Evidence beyond the documents: earns the point for describing a specific relevant example not in the documents, such as the Female Moral Reform Society, the Seneca Falls Convention, or the temperance movement.
rubric.notEarned: A vague reference to outside knowledge with no specific example does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Sourcing: earns the point for explaining how the audience, purpose, historical situation, or point of view of at least two documents shapes the argument.
rubric.notEarned: Naming a document's author without explaining how it shapes the argument does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Complexity: earns the point for a complex argument, such as qualifying the thesis by showing where reform changed society and where its reach stopped, or who it included and left out.
rubric.notEarned: A second example with no qualification or weighing does not earn the point.

modelOutline:
Thesis: The abolition movement transformed the debate over slavery to a great extent between 1817 and 1860, turning a quiet question of gradual emancipation into a loud moral and political fight, yet it did not end slavery, and its opponents answered with censorship and violence.
Context: The Second Great Awakening gave reformers a perfectionist faith, while the cotton boom made slavery richer and more entrenched in the South.
Evidence for transformation: Walker's Appeal and Garrison's Liberator made immediatism public; Grimké carried it into women's rights; the Fugitive Slave Act dragged the debate into Northern towns and turned indifferent Northerners into abolitionists.
Evidence for limits: a mob killed Lovejoy in 1837, Southern states banned abolitionist papers, and the Supreme Court ruled in Dred Scott (1857) that Black people were not citizens and had no rights that white men were bound to respect.
Complexity: Abolitionism transformed the debate by forcing the nation to argue about slavery in moral terms, even as its enemies proved the debate itself had become dangerous.
